szoveg_eredeti:
Researchers Propose Calibrated Safeguard Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Scientific Writing

An integrative review of biomedical informatics literature has produced a comprehensive operational framework designed to govern the deployment of generative artificial intelligence across health sciences manuscript preparation. Published in Informatics in Medicine Unlocked by José Daniel Sánchez Redrobán, Vanessa Romero Durán, and Mario Rivera, the study introduces the Generative AI-Assisted Writing Framework for Researchers, abbreviated as GAIA-Write. The investigators synthesized empirical studies, computational evaluations, and international editorial guidelines to construct an end-to-end operational architecture. The proposed system directly couples every phase of scientific drafting with calibrated task delegation boundaries, an obligatory pre-flight data confidentiality audit, and a mandatory three-tier quality control verification gate. By anchoring procedural safeguards to empirically observed technical failure modes rather than abstract prohibitions, the authors establish actionable boundaries intended to preserve the factual precision, ethical transparency, and cognitive rigor of published health research.

The rapid emergence of consumer-facing large language models following the public debut of OpenAI’s ChatGPT in November 2022 initiated a profound transformation across academic writing environments. Natural language processing platforms quickly evolved from specialized computational instruments into ubiquitous drafting assistants, driving measurable shifts in vocabulary patterns across indexed medical literature. In clinical disciplines, adoption has been characterized as swift yet persistently underreported, with formal analyses revealing undisclosed usage in specialized dental journals and active utilization among university faculty in resource-constrained environments such as sub-Saharan Africa. Within medical informatics, generative platforms operate simultaneously as algorithmic information processors and cognitive collaborators. This dual identity generates a sharp operational tension: while generative systems demonstrably enhance initial text generation speed and help overcome linguistic hurdles for non-native English scholars, their probabilistic architectures introduce severe vulnerabilities, including artificial hallucinations, fabricated citations, epistemic distortions, and potential cognitive dependency among investigators.

To evaluate these dynamics systematically, the researchers executed an integrative review adhering to the five-stage methodology established by Whittemore and Knafl, encompassing problem identification, comprehensive literature searching, data evaluation, multi-step analysis, and presentation. Literature queries were conducted across four major electronic databases—PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar—spanning publications from January 1, 2022, through February 15, 2026. The initial bibliographic retrieval yielded 1482 records, which were subsequently refined through automated and duplicate removal down to 1128 unique citations. Screening of titles and abstracts excluded 1030 non-relevant papers, leaving 98 full-text records for detailed appraisal. Applying strict criteria regarding operational relevance to manuscript preparation, the team excluded 56 publications and identified 42 core sources, citing 41 distinct works comprising 11 experimental evaluations of model outputs, four observational or bibliometric surveys, two comparative policy evaluations, 16 narrative reviews or commentaries, four published taxonomies or checklists, three primary editorial statements, and one preprint.

The synthesis of evaluative literature demonstrated that machine drafting capabilities are concentrated in preliminary outlining, structural organization, and draft expansion. Evaluative studies such as the Clinical Research with LLM-Generated Writing trial documented notable time savings when clinicians refined model-generated preliminary observational drafts under human supervisory control. Similar utility was observed in drafting structured reproductive medicine manuscripts and generating initial outlines. However, comparative trials revealed critical substantive disparities between machine-generated and human-authored prose. In comparative investigations analyzing plastic surgery abstracts, text generated by artificial intelligence exhibited superior readability indices and syntactic consistency but frequently omitted vital clinical granularity and methodological nuance. Likewise, case report evaluations demonstrated that purely autonomous machine drafting lacked diagnostic balance, whereas supervised hybrid human-machine workflows achieved the highest reader acceptance and clinical accuracy, reinforcing that autonomous drafting cannot substitute for clinician expertise.

In the domain of literature review and evidence synthesis, the synthesis emphasized a fundamental architectural distinction between general-purpose conversational models and domain-specialized academic tools. Uncritical reliance on standard autoregressive language models consistently produces severe bibliographic distortions, generating fictitious author lists, non-resolving digital object identifiers, and fabricated biochemical findings due to next-token prediction mechanisms that lack real-time database indexation. Conversely, specialized research discovery platforms—such as Elicit, SciSpace, Consensus, and Semantic Scholar—integrate underlying language models with live bibliographic indexing and retrieval-augmented generation. By anchoring synthesized summaries directly to indexed PubMed and Crossref corpora, these specialized retrieval-augmented tools substantially mitigate citation fabrication. Nevertheless, the investigators noted that retrieval-augmented generation does not eliminate the requirement for human oversight, because researchers must still retrieve and independently examine full-text primary articles to ensure retrieved sources genuinely support synthesized assertions.

Investigations into linguistic translation and stylistic refinement revealed that multi-language translation and grammatical correction represent the most technically mature capabilities of modern language models. Empirical assessments demonstrated high semantic fidelity during cross-lingual translation of specialized surgical manuscripts, alongside significant utility in correcting grammatical anomalies, enhancing academic register, and restructuring non-idiomatic prose for researchers communicating in a second language. However, the review identified subtle linguistic hazards termed silent semantic drift. Language models frequently exhibit an erosion of epistemic hedging, automatically transforming cautious correlational qualifiers such as ‘suggests a possible association’ into definitive causal declarations such as ‘directly causes.’ Furthermore, models regularly introduce inappropriate synonym substitutions, replacing standardized clinical entities such as ‘adverse event’ with colloquial variants such as ‘negative effect,’ while flattening critical caveats concerning sample representativeness and statistical power.

Beyond linguistic considerations, the integrative review synthesized acute risks concerning biostatistical analysis, research governance, cognitive development, and international publication ethics. Descriptive informatics vignettes showed that while code-capable models can assist in writing statistical scripts in R or Python, they lack numerical comprehension and frequently misapply statistical distribution assumptions, such as applying parametric tests to skewed non-parametric datasets. In terms of governance, transmitting unpublished clinical datasets, research protocols, or embargoed peer reviews to commercial cloud systems creates critical data protection violations under regulations such as HIPA
